title: Rewiring Britain: The Andy Burnham Project
author: Graham Peebles
content:
"The change we are planning will be the biggest change in our lifetimes to the
way the country is run." So [said](https://andyburnham.org.uk/2026/07/20/andy-
burnham-speech-at-the-peoples-history-museum-manchester-29-june-2026/) Andy
Burnham on 29 June, a month before becoming the new UK Prime Minister.

His vision includes a more streamlined state with a clearer purpose. A new
Prime Minister's office based in Manchester – No.10 North – "will be the
conduit through which we redistribute power and resources across the UK. It
will coordinate all parts of government, at national and local level, to agree
on a long-term economic strategy."

"It [No.10 North] will be given a mission to strive for equivalent living
conditions in all parts of Britain" — a principle borrowed from the German
Basic Law, the [constitution](https://www.gesetze-im-
internet.de/englisch_gg/englisch_gg.html) of the Federal Republic of Germany.

"No.10 North will support the regions on three clear tasks: Reform of
essential utilities; Re-industrialisation; And the regeneration of places."

Burnham has pledged to deliver a 10-year plan to renew Britain and reform its
troubled politics – a plan that includes ending rough sleeping, reforming
education, and tackling social care.

This means breaking with the corrosive ideology of the past 40 years, a period
in which Thatcherism, in varying degrees, has shaped, and poisoned, the socio-
economic order; fuelling division, promoting greed, and fermenting resentment.

**From Mayor to PM**

Andy Burnham began his political career in 1994 as a researcher for the late
Labour MP Tessa Jowell. He later became a special adviser (1998–2001) within
Tony Blair's government, a role he held until his election as an MP in 2001.

He speaks with sincerity and passion, and comes across as "normal": someone
you could have a coffee with – or a beer – and talk to about anything: rising
prices, renting a flat, deciding on a career, music, or football.

From 2017 until becoming MP for Makerfield on 26 June, he was Mayor of
Manchester (or "some town", as Donald Trump ignorantly called it) – a decade
in which he built a reputation for competence and empathy that set him apart
from the Westminster establishment. After winning the by-election, he was
swiftly elected leader of the Labour Party, ousting Sir Keir Starmer, and
subsequently, on 20 July, Andy Burnham became Prime Minister.

Upon entering Downing Street, he appointed a cabinet with a record 12 women,
and purged many of Starmer's allies, including some of the most ardent
supporters of Israel.

In the UK's parliamentary system, voters choose a party, not a leader – so,
despite far-right carping, there is no constitutional need for a new election.

The current electoral cycle runs until August 2029, giving Burnham and his
team just three years to bring about meaningful change. However, he has the
latitude to call an early election if he judges it beneficial. Assuming Labour
were to win, an early election would free Burnham and his team from Starmer's
restrictive fiscal commitments, potentially creating opportunities for more
radical policies.

**Clear vision**

Despite attempts by opposition parties and right-wing media to present Burnham
as someone who "flip-flops," his priorities have remained consistent for
years.

In Head North, [co-authored](https://www.waterstones.com/book/head-north/andy-
burnham/steve-rotheram/9781398719743) with Steve Rotheram – the Mayor of
Liverpool City Region – he lays out a ten-point plan to "rewire Britain": a
written constitution, proportional representation (instead of first-past-the-
post), full devolution to regions and nations, two equal education paths
(academic and technical), a national social housing programme, a Hillsborough
Law – since introduced – and a net-zero re-industrialisation of the North of
England, embracing 21st-century industries like data centres, AI, and
renewable energy.

He has repeatedly spoken about bringing utilities (water, energy,
telecommunications, transport) – all sold off under Thatcher – back under
public control. England is the only country with a fully privatised water
system, and re-nationalisation has widespread public support – something
Burnham has advocated for decades.

What is lacking to date in Burnham's plans is a foreign policy agenda – one
that includes closer ties with the EU (ideally with the aim of re-joining the
customs union); a more compassionate immigration policy; a commitment to
increase the overseas aid budget, cut under Keir Starmer's premiership; and a
clear, responsible environmental framework.

**Beyond Cynicism and Division**

Burnham is right to lay most, if not all, of the issues facing Britain at the
feet of the ideological dogma of Neo-Liberalism, and its most fervent devotee,
Margaret Thatcher (UK Prime Minister 1979–1990). Thatcher famously declared
that "there is no such thing as society" – a statement that legitimised
selfishness, fed individualism, and eroded community unity.

Since Thatcher – with the relative exception of Tony Blair's New Labour
government (1997–2007), when inequality slowed and investment in public
services increased significantly – inequalities of all kinds have grown:
income and wealth, education and opportunities, access to culture and
employment, and regional disparities.

In relation to the most basic form of inequality – wealth and income – the
number of billionaires in the UK has risen from 15 in 1990 to 165 in 2024, one
in four of whom, according to the Equality Trust, draw wealth from property
and inheritance that contributes nearly nothing to the real economy. At the
same time, poverty has increased significantly, with 4.5 million children, or
one in three, said to be living in poverty.

Inequality of all kinds is an expression of social injustice and Neo-
Liberalism, an extreme form of capitalism that sees everyone as a consumer and
everything as an object to be consumed, strengthens every area of inequality.

One of the central tenets of its propaganda – that 'trickle-down economics' is
the most effective way of spreading wealth – is a complete fantasy; the very
opposite is true – wealth flows upwards, with the already rich (people,
regions, nations) becoming richer and richer.

Andy Burnham not only recognises this but has openly spoken about it as a
fundamental cause of the social and economic misery that millions of people in
the UK feel: the lack of hope, and the devastating impact on the nation's
mental health, particularly among under-35s, many of whom cannot find work.

The consequences are stark, particularly in post-industrial towns and cities,
where such despair has fuelled racism and division, driving some into the arms
of the far right. Whipped up by right-wing lies and distortions, amplified by
a compliant media, division has become the dominant political currency in many
of these communities - hence Brexit.

**Rebuilding Society**

Burnham's entire project is a repudiation of all this, of all that Thatcher
and her creed stood for, and stand for. It is an attempt to create greater
social justice, to spread opportunities and create economic
[growth](https://andyburnham.org.uk/2026/07/20/andy-burnham-speech-at-the-
peoples-history-museum-manchester-29-june-2026/) throughout the country –
"good growth in every postcode and hope in every heart"; to rebuild the idea
of society through a reimagined state that places cooperation, fairness, and
collective endeavour at its core.

Redistribution must be at the heart of the Burnham project: redistributing
wealth through a tax on assets (one that is not territorially tied) on the
very rich, and taxing bank profits; spreading opportunity across the regions
via genuine devolution, which gives mayors and councils real control of their
area; and creating a culture of innovation and sharing, so that everyone
benefits, not just the few.

This means ensuring that secure, well-paid work, good housing, and education
choice (as promised) are available in all parts of the country. Such a shift
would stand in direct contrast with prevailing attitudes and the current
system, which hoards opportunity in the capital, leaves millions in insecure
work, fuels division, and enriches a super-rich elite whose wealth contributes
nearly nothing to the real economy.

People are crying out for such a shift: for economic and social justice, for
better housing, for good, well-paid work, and for broad-based inclusive
education.

Tangible change will inevitably take time, but the shift in tone and approach
already seen from Burnham and his government is igniting a spark of hope
across the country.

This is a moment of enormous national significance, which should not be
underestimated. A chance to reverse decades of state cruelty, neglect, and
injustice; to prove that politics and governments, when rooted in principles
of goodness, can bring lasting change, improving the lives of the majority of
people and creating a kinder society at ease with itself.

Andy Burnham, we wish you well.
